summary: Clarify how token refill windows and concurrency buckets interact when using short-lived/ephemeral keys for parallel ingest
description:
Issue summary: Customer is seeing spikes of 429s during large parallel ingests which use short-lived signed API keys. They reported that the 429s occur after a flurry of successful requests and correlate with the signed-key refresh process.

Impact: Intermittent ingestion failures (10-25% of batches) for nightly backfills. Customer reports increased latency and failed retries impacting downstream processing and causing missed SLA windows.

Environment: Dedicated pool (customer-owned reserved GPUs) in us-west, pool scaled to expected capacity. Workload: 400 parallel workers creating short-lived signed API keys per upload job, each key used for 30-90s and then rotated.

Steps to reproduce (customer-provided):
1) Start 400 parallel uploader processes.
2) Each process requests a signed key for a 60s TTL.
3) Each process performs a burst of 50 small embedding calls over HTTP/1.1 then rotates key.
4) Observe 429s in response stream starting ~15 minutes into the job.

Logs/headers: Customer captured rate-limit response headers from a failing request: 
- x-rate-limit-limit: 1200
- x-rate-limit-remaining: 0
- x-rate-limit-reset: 21
- x-rate-limit-window: 60s
- x-rate-limit-scope: tenant

Their tooling shows windows opening/closing aligned with signed-key refresh timestamps. They believe requests served through different edge NAT IPs may be double-counted against tenant windows.

Customer ask: Clarify how token refill windows, per-API-key buckets, and per-connection/concurrency buckets interact when short-lived keys are frequently created and reused across many client processes. They want recommended config or best practices for large parallel uploads on Dedicated pools.

investigation_notes: Checked tenant token-bucket metrics for LexiForms during incident window: observed periodic drops to 0 remaining tokens on tenant window every ~60s, consistent with a tenant-level refill window of 60s and heavy parallel consumption.

Edge logs show many ephemeral keys routed via a small set of NATed IPs due to egress pooling on customer side; ingress counters show duplicate counting at edge and origin layers because key rotation triggered new connection establishment that hits per-connection concurrency accounting in our proxy layer.

Hypothesis 1: Frequent key creation causes many short-lived token buckets to be created in the rate-limiter in quick succession; refill alignment plus simultaneous consumption can cause tenant window exhaustion even though per-key quotas appear adequate.

Hypothesis 2: Proxy/edge-level connection reuse with HTTP/1.1 pipelining caused our counting layer to treat some parallel streams as separate quota consumers, contributing to faster depletion of effective concurrency slots.

Metric artifacts: 'tenant_window_consumption' spike plot, 'per_key_bucket_create_rate' spiked during startup. Linked to PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/rate-limiter/pull/482 for additional telemetry added.
Test run (2026-03-12 22:00): Customer performed controlled run with TTL=600s and jittered issuance; observed 95% reduction in 429s in that window. This supports TTL alignment hypothesis.

SRE note: For Dedicated pools, there is a tenant-level refill and optional per-key smoothing. The platform currently defaults to a tight tenant window for predictable billing. We can enable 'ephemeral smoothing' toggle for dedicated tier to smooth per-key short-lived bursts.
Recorded similar behavior in older tickets (linked SUP-314159) related to multi-region ingest and refill alignment.
resolution:
Workaround and recommendations provided: 1) Increase signed-key TTL for large parallel upload jobs (recommended 5-15 minutes) to reduce churn in token-bucket bookkeeping. 2) Add jitter to key issuance (random 0-30s) to avoid synchronized refill boundaries. 3) If using HTTP/1.1 multiplexing, consider switching to HTTP/2 or reusing persistent connections to reduce per-connection counting artifacts. 4) Support enabled a tenant-level 'ephemeral smoothing' flag in staging for LexiForms to be trialed; this smooths token refill attribution across short-lived keys.

Permanent follow-ups: SRE to propose a config toggle in Dedicated console for ephemeral smoothing and document recommended defaults for short-lived keys; work item created in internal backlog (INT-99812) to add server-side heuristic to detect large ephemeral-key fanout and automatically enable smoothing.

Status: Customer verified A/B test (TTL increase + jitter) improved success rate; we are scheduling an engineering rollout plan for the smoothing toggle. Ticket will be closed after rollout and confirmation of reduction in 429s over a full nightly backfill cycle.
